records.title: Distributor internal shaft seal fails, oil leaks into cap and causes misfires + stalling
records.description: The ignition distributor on 1990-2001 Integras (and all Honda B-series engines of the era) sits at the rear of the head and is driven directly off the exhaust cam. Inside the distributor housing, an oil seal separates the cam-driven shaft from the cap/rotor/electrical assembly above it. When this seal hardens with age and heat cycling, engine oil under pressure leaks past the shaft, fills the cap area, and coats the rotor and contacts. Result: misfires, hard starts, hesitation, stalling at idle, and sometimes a check-engine light for misfire codes. The shaft seal CAN technically be replaced internally, but it is difficult and many shops will not attempt it — they replace the whole distributor instead because reused housings often re-leak quickly. Cleaning the cap helps for a few weeks and then symptoms return.
records.solution: Replace the complete distributor. OEM Honda distributors are pricey ($350-500+) but reliable; aftermarket units from Cardone, A1 Cardone, or Spectra Premium are $80-150 and work fine for non-track use. While the distributor is out, also replace the cap, rotor, and ignition wires — they're cheap and replacing them at the same time saves a labor cycle. After install, time the engine to factory spec (16°±2° BTDC at idle with timing-adjust connector unplugged). Do NOT just clean the cap and call it done — the oil keeps coming and you'll be back in 6 weeks. If you're keeping the car long-term, the Honda OEM distributor outlasts aftermarket 2:1.
symptoms: Oil pooling visibly inside the distributor cap when removed
Engine misfires intermittently, especially under load or after warm-up
Stalling at idle once the engine is hot
Hard start when warm (oil-fouled rotor won't conduct)
Check engine light with P0301-P0304 misfire codes
Briefly improves after distributor cleaning, returns within weeks

records.title: 3.0CL automatic transmission slips and fails — flush is forbidden, filter is not serviceable
records.description: The 1997-1999 3.0CL uses an automatic transmission specific to its V6 model family (the 2.2CL/2.3CL 4-cylinder variants do NOT share this transmission and are not affected). Owners and independent transmission shops widely report failures: slipping under load, not shifting out of 1st until warm, harsh shifts, and eventually total failure. Reports of repeat failures are common. NOTE: this transmission failure pattern is more severe and better documented on the 2nd-gen 3.2CL (2001-2003) than on the 1st-gen 3.0CL; the 1st-gen exhibits the same underlying weakness but at lower failure rates. A critical maintenance detail: this transmission has minimal internal filtration, and the filter is not serviceable without complete teardown. Owners who power-flush a slipping unit dislodge clutch debris and accelerate the failure rather than fix it.
records.solution: If symptoms appear, immediately switch to ONLY Acura/Honda ATF (never Dextron substitute) and start a regular drain-and-refill schedule at every engine oil change interval (6 months). Do NOT power-flush — this transmission has effectively no serviceable filter and pressurized flushing forces debris through tight passages. If slipping has already started, a transmission specialist (not a quick-lube) needs to drop the pan to check for clutch material in the fluid. Once debris is visible, only a rebuild fixes it ($2,500-3,500). Replacements/rebuilds may need a fresh torque converter — the original is a known weak point. Add an aftermarket transmission cooler at rebuild time; the factory cooling is undersized.
symptoms: Transmission won't shift out of 1st until engine is warm
Slipping in higher gears under load
Rough or delayed engagement from Park to Drive
Harsh thunk shifts when slowing
Burnt smell from transmission dipstick
Repeat failures within 30,000-60,000 miles after replacement

records.title: Ignition cylinder wear → shift interlock fails → rollaway risk (NHTSA recall 03V423000, 2003)
records.description: NHTSA Campaign ID 03V423000 (October 2003) covers 1998-1999 Acura CL models. The defect: the ignition cylinder body wears, which causes the shift interlock to malfunction. If the vehicle does not securely lock in Park because the worn cylinder allows the interlock to disengage, the vehicle can roll away even with the transmission in any non-Park position. This is distinct from NHTSA Campaign 02V120000 (2002), which covered 1997-1998 CL for a different ignition switch defect. The 1998-1999 model years are the overlap between the two recalls — those owners should check both campaign IDs against their VIN. The fix is a free dealer replacement of the ignition switch/cylinder assembly. As of 2026, safety recalls have no expiration date under 49 CFR §573.6, so eligible VINs can still be repaired free of charge.
records.solution: Check VIN at owners.acura.com/recalls or NHTSA recall lookup to confirm whether your specific car was included. If yes, schedule the free dealer fix — they replace the interlock assembly in about 30 min. If your dealer claims the recall is 'closed' or 'no longer covered,' escalate to American Honda Customer Service (800-382-2238) — safety recalls have no expiration date under federal law (49 CFR §573.6). If you can't get to a dealer, ALWAYS verify the shifter is fully in Park and the parking brake is set before removing the key. This is not a workaround — it's a discipline check that protects you while you arrange the free repair.

Shift lever stays freely movable after key is removed

records.title: Engine motor mounts crack and collapse — drivetrain vibration + clunk on shifts
records.description: All DA and DC Integras (and all Honda B-series transverse cars) use four hydraulic engine mounts: front, rear, passenger-side (the 'side mount'), and driver-side (the transmission mount). The rear and front mounts use a fluid-filled rubber bushing that wears out — typically the rear mount goes first by 100,000 miles, the passenger-side side mount second. Failure signs: clunk when shifting in or out of gear (especially on automatics), vibration at idle that disappears when you press the brake or shift to neutral, and a 'wheel hop' feeling under hard acceleration. Skipping motor mount replacement on a manual Integra accelerates wear on the half-shafts, transmission shift forks, and the trans itself, because the engine is moving around in the bay.
records.solution: Replace mounts one at a time as they fail, not all four preemptively (the front and side mounts can last 200k+). Diagnose by having a helper rev the engine in neutral while you look — a healthy mount holds the engine still; a dead one lets the engine rock 1-2 inches. Common pattern: rear mount + passenger-side mount are the first two to need replacement, and both are visible from above without lifting. Aftermarket options range from cheap rubber ($30 each) to Energy Suspension polyurethane ($60-100, transmits more vibration but lasts forever) to Innovative Mounts billet ($100-200, used for tracked cars). For a daily-driver Integra, OEM Honda rubber or Cardone is the right balance. Total cost replacing rear + side: $80-300 in parts, 2-3 hours of labor.
symptoms: Clunk or thud when shifting between Drive and Reverse (auto)
Clunk on engagement of 1st gear from stop (manual)
Vibration at idle that subsides when brake is pressed or trans is in Neutral
Wheel hop or chassis shudder under hard launches
Visible engine rock when revved in neutral
Visible cracks, separation, or fluid leakage on the mount itself

records.title: Outer CV joint boot tears leading to joint failure and clicking
records.description:
The CV joints are lubricated with grease and sealed inside rubber boots that hold the grease in and keep dirt out; over time the boots crack or tear, grease escapes and dirt enters the joint causing it to break down, and the joint develops excessive play in its bearings, producing a repetitive clicking sound when accelerating through a curve.
 
Clicking or popping noise when turning is the classic sign of a worn outer CV joint, most obvious during sharp low-speed turns like in a parking lot; vibrations while accelerating and dark heavy grease splattered on the inner edge of the tire are additional symptoms.
 Common on the B18A1-powered DA chassis where the outer boots crack with age and especially after donuts in reverse or hard cornering.
records.solution:
If the boot has just torn and no elements got into the joint, regreasing and rebooting can work — a $10 boot kit vs. a $60 replacement axle is the tradeoff.
 
Reman axles run around $50 each and boot kits about $25 — AutoZone and similar carry both for the 1992 Integra 1.8L DOHC.
 
Pack outer CV joint boot with molybdenum disulfide grease, lube the spider and inside bore of rollers, ensure rollers are aligned with marks made at disassembly and install with the high side of rollers facing outward.
 Use new boot clamps (low-profile metal bands included in kit). Most owners simply swap the full reman half-shaft for under $100/side — quicker than rebooting. Always replace the axle nut and use a new transaxle retaining ring.
symptoms: Clicking or popping when turning at low speed
Grease splattered on inner wheel and suspension
Clunk on acceleration or shifting into gear
Vibration at highway speed
Torn or cracked outer boot visible at full lock

records.title: Ignitor / ignition control module inside the distributor fails — intermittent or no-start
records.description: The Integra's ignition system uses a discrete ignitor module (also called ignition control module, or ICM) mounted inside the distributor cap. The module triggers the coil and is a known failure point on 1990-2001 Integras — replacement units are stocked by most major parts retailers (Beck Arnley, Delphi, Standard Motor Products). Failure presents as a no-spark condition: engine cranks normally but will not start, or starts intermittently. Often happens after the engine reaches operating temperature, then the car will not restart until the module cools — though owners report the failure mode varies. NOTE: 1990-1993 Integras use the OBD-0 diagnostic system, which produces numeric flash codes (e.g. code 15 for ignition) rather than the OBD-II P-codes used from 1996+. The original Honda heat sink part #30121-PM5-A02 mentioned in some installation guides is now discontinued/out of production.
records.solution: Test the ignitor before replacing — a multimeter check at the coil primary terminals while cranking will confirm whether the module is sending pulse to the coil. If no pulse: replace. OEM Honda module $80-150, aftermarket (Beck Arnley, Delphi) $30-80. The module sits inside the distributor cap; replacement requires removing the cap and rotor, unscrewing 2 mounting screws, and transferring the heat sink if present (Civic/Integra units may require heat sink #30121-PM5-A02 for correct fitment). Inspect the inside of the distributor cap and rotor for moisture or corrosion while you're in there — a cracked cap allows water in and causes premature module failure on the replacement. Replace cap + rotor at the same time as a preventive measure.
symptoms: Engine cranks but won't start (no spark to coil)
Intermittent no-start, especially when hot
Sudden stall while driving with no warning
Check engine light with P0300-series misfire codes
Engine starts, runs briefly, then dies
Restart works after the car cools for 30-60 minutes

Test before replacing. Use a multimeter on the coil primary terminals while cranking — if the module is pulsing the coil, the no-start is somewhere else (often the main relay).

records.title: Motorized passive shoulder belt sticks on track or fails to move
records.description:
US-market 1990-1993 Integras used a motorized passive shoulder belt that travels on a track from the A-pillar to the B-pillar. 
A common failure has the auto belt stuck in the down/forward position with the warning light staying on; pulling it back manually doesn't help because once the door is opened and closed it goes back down but won't return.
 
Symptoms include intermittent retraction — sometimes 100%, sometimes 0%, sometimes stopping partway — accompanied by a constant error beep indicating a seatbelt malfunction.
 Failure modes include blown 30A passive-motor fuses, broken door-jamb switches, worn track gears, and seized motors.
records.solution:
The seat-belt fuses are under the hood on the passenger-side shock tower — the fuse-box cover labels them; pull and inspect the passive motor L and R fuses (30A each) first.
 
Manually unstick the belt by locating the rod with a hex-head fitting on the motor, then use a screwdriver/Allen key to drive the seat-belt motor manually to the rear position before closing the door.
 
American Acura/Honda has a policy of offering a lifetime warranty on the functional components of their seat belts — as long as the vehicle is an American-market car, has not been in a collision, and the belt assembly has not been modified, American Acura will fix it at their cost; if the dealer refuses, phone Acura Client Relations at (800) 382-2238.
 Note that Honda Canada does not honor this policy.
symptoms: Shoulder belt stuck in forward (door) position
Belt fails to return when door closes
Constant warning chime/beep
Seat belt warning light stays on
Motor audibly hums but belt doesn't move
Belt retracts only intermittently

records.title: Passenger-side cowl seal leak floods blower motor and floor pan
records.description:
A very common problem on 90-93 Integras where, after many years, the foam seals beneath the windshield cowl no longer keep water out and it ends up on the passenger floor after passing through the blower motor and rusting it out.
 
The drainage paths beneath the cowl are very shallow and are easily clogged with accumulated dust and leaf matter; one drainage path runs right over the hole where the blower sucks in air, so if there is a blockage downstream rainwater pours right into the blower assembly.
 Drivers see soaked passenger carpet, foggy windshield, musty smell, and eventually a dead blower motor or resistor.
records.solution:
Order eight of Honda part number 91608-SJ6-003 (the clear grommet/seal pieces) from a Honda or Acura dealer — they are inexpensive at roughly $2.50 each.
 Remove the wiper arms (14mm) and the black plastic cowl, clear out all leaf debris from the drainage channels, then replace the old foam strip with new urethane weatherstripping and reinstall with the new grommets. 
Remove the wipers, pop the 7-8 pins, undo the pins along the perimeter under the hood, clean out the drainage paths, scrape out the old weather stripping, and replace with 1/4" wide, 1/2" thick urethane weather stripping for a permanent fix.
 If the blower motor or resistor has already corroded, replace those at the same time.
symptoms: Wet passenger-side floor mat after rain
Water sprays from vents when blower is turned on
Musty/mildew interior smell
Foggy windshield that won't clear
Blower motor dead or noisy
Rusted blower motor housing

communityRecommendations.content: Order 8x Honda P/N 91608-SJ6-003 grommets before starting — they're cheap (~$2.50 each) and you'll destroy the originals on removal.
If the blower has been getting wet for a while, plan on also replacing the blower motor and the resistor — water corrodes both.

records.title: PGM-FI main relay solder joint cracks cause hot-weather no-start
records.description:
The PGM-FI Main Relay is a critical electronic switch that sends power to the fuel pump and engine computer (ECU); when you turn the key it clicks on, allowing the pump to build pressure and the computer to manage the engine — without a working main relay the engine won't get fuel or the electronic commands it needs to run.
 
The main relay is a known weak point on DA-chassis Integras — over many years the solder joints inside the relay crack from heat and vibration, and the problem is often worse on hot days or after the car has been running, as heat causes the cracked joints to expand and lose connection.
 Symptoms include crank-but-no-start after the car sits in the sun, intermittent stalling, and the fuel pump failing to prime audibly when the key is turned to ON.
records.solution:
Replacing the main relay is one of the easiest repairs on the Integra; it is located under the driver's-side dash, near the hood release lever and to the right of the parking brake pedal — unbolt the mounting bracket (10mm), unplug the harness, and plug in the new relay.
 
Use a quality replacement — the DA-chassis OEM part number is typically 39400-PM6-003 (verify with your VIN at an Acura dealer or parts store, as several supersessions exist). Reputable aftermarket cross-references include Standard Motor Products RY-passenger-style relays, Beck/Arnley, and Denso. Expect to pay $25-$80 for the part and avoid the cheapest generic relays — reliability matters.
 
Resoldering the cracked joints on the existing relay's circuit board has been done successfully by many owners, but requires skill with a soldering iron and may not be permanent — a new aftermarket relay is the more reliable repair.
symptoms: Engine cranks but won't start when hot
No fuel pump prime sound at key-on
Intermittent stalling while driving
Restarts fine after cooling down
Check engine light may not flash codes if relay is dead

records.title: Rear quarter panel and rocker panel rust-through behind wheel arch protectors
records.description:
Any Integra that still has the rear wheel arch protectors is already starting to rust, even if not visible on the outside — pulling a protector typically reveals wet mud trapped against the inner arch lip with rust eating the metal underneath.
 
This is one of the most common problems on 90's Hondas; it happens on Integras, Civics and Preludes, and the rust bubbles up around the bumper bolt area requiring it to be ground or cut out.
 Owners in salt-belt and humid regions see bubbling paint at the rear wheel arch lip, holes through rocker panels, and structural rust that fails safety inspection.
records.solution:
All G2 Integras came with rear wheel arch protectors — pull them off as preventive maintenance; Acura wanted around $40-$50 each for them new.
 For early rust, cut out affected metal with at least one inch of clean margin, treat the inner frame with a rust converter such as POR-15, and weld in patch panels (92-95 Civic patch panels can be modified to fit). 
Proper repair is to replace the complete rear quarter — body shop estimates run around $4000 for both sides with paint; DIY gutting/stripping can drop it closer to $2000-$3500.
 Aftermarket wheel arch and quarter patch panels are available from Mill Supply and other restoration vendors.
symptoms: Paint bubbling at rear wheel arch lip
Holes visible in rocker panel behind side skirt
Rust bubbling around rear bumper bolt area
Wet mud/debris trapped behind plastic arch protectors
Fails safety/MOT inspection

records.title: Rear wheel bearing hum from press-in hub assembly
records.description:
The wheel bearings on the 1990-1993 Acura Integra (DA chassis, second generation) are critical parts located inside the wheel hub assembly — for the DA-generation Integra these are press-in style bearings pressed into the steering knuckle in the front and the hub/spindle in the rear, and they support the full weight of the car while it's in motion.
 
When a wheel bearing starts to go bad it usually gives warning signs; ignoring them can lead to serious problems including the wheel separating from the car, and the most common sign is a humming, rumbling, or grinding sound that gets louder with speed.
 
The hum is often hard to localize from inside the cabin — passengers in the back may each think it's on their side — but it typically lessens when steering loads the bad bearing's opposite side (e.g., turning right unloads the left side, so if noise decreases when turning right, the left bearing is likely the culprit).
records.solution:
This is an advanced DIY job. Some owners replace the rear as a complete pre-pressed hub assembly (commonly $80-$120 from aftermarket suppliers), which avoids press work; others source just the bearing/race and press it into the spindle/knuckle using a hydraulic shop press (or have a machine shop do it). Front bearings on the DA always require pressing into the knuckle.
 Quality replacement brands include SKF, Timken, FAG, Koyo and NSK (the latter two are often OEM suppliers to Honda).
 Rear bearings are a bit more expensive but easier to access than the fronts.
 Budget $40-$120 per bearing/assembly plus press/labor; total shop cost typically $200-$450 per corner.
symptoms: Humming or rumbling noise that increases with speed
Noise changes pitch or volume when turning
Vibration through floor at highway speed
Slight wheel play when rocked on jack stands
Uneven inner tire wear

For the rear, you can often buy a complete pre-assembled hub/bearing unit for roughly $80-$120, which avoids needing access to a hydraulic press.
Stick with Koyo or NSK bearings — they were the original Honda OEM suppliers and outlast most cheap aftermarket kits.

records.title: 4-speed automatic: shift solenoid failure causes D4 light flash, missed shifts, and limp mode
records.description:
The Honda BAXA/MAXA 4-speed automatic in the Integra is notoriously sensitive to fluid condition and shift-solenoid contamination. Solenoid A/B failure causes flashing D4 light, harsh or missed 2-3/3-4 shifts, loss of power in D4/D3, and sometimes speedometer drop-out. 
Integra often faces delayed or missed shifts and manual downshifting difficulties in automatic transmissions. Shifting problems in the 1998 Integra's automatic transmission can stem from a clogged transmission filter or screen restricting fluid flow. This causes poor hydraulic pressure, leading to missed 4th gear shifts and failure to downshift.
 
While driving, the D4 suddenly lost almost all power, wouldn't shift, and the speedometer stopped working. Codes returned were Automatic Transaxle FI A circuit failure and ELD error.
records.solution:
Drain-and-fill with Honda ATF-Z1/DW-1 (NEVER use generic Dexron — it will destroy the clutches). 
The transmission fluid in the Integra 4AT's are supposed to be changed every 3 years/36,000 mi. It can cook and wear out just like the oil in your engine.

records.title: Timing belt failure on interference B18 engine bends valves
records.description:
All B18 engines in the 1994-2001 Integra (DC2/DB7) are interference-design. If the timing belt snaps (or jumps teeth from a seized tensioner or water pump), pistons strike open valves. The belt should be replaced every 90,000 miles along with the water pump, tensioner, and seals.
The timing belt in the DOHC Honda engine keeps the engine running and valvetrain events on time. Because the 1.8 liter B18 engine is an interference engine, failure of the timing belt usually means pistons have hit valves. This can lead to lack of cylinder compression at the bare minimum. At worst the valve may become stuck or destroy the piston.
records.solution:
Replace the complete timing belt kit: belt, tensioner, tensioner spring, water pump, cam and crank seals, and balance shaft belt where applicable.
Non-VTEC LS (B18B1) timing belt part numbers are 14400-P7J-004 or 14400-PR4-A01, paired with the 19-tooth water pump 19200-P75-003 / 19200-PT5-000 / 19200-PT5-003. The VTEC GSR (B18C1) uses timing belt 14400-P72-004 / 14400-P72-014 paired with a 22-tooth water pump.
Do NOT mix LS and GSR water pumps — the tooth counts differ (19T vs 22T) and the belts are different lengths.
Professional cost for preventive replacement: approximately $350-600. Post-failure repair (valve job / head rebuild) can reach $2,000-3,000+.

records.title: Timing belt must be replaced at 90,000 mi / 72 months — interference engine eats valves if it snaps
records.description: The Legend's C27A (1990) and C32A (1991-1995) V6s are both interference engines: the valves and pistons share the same vertical space at different points in the rotation, separated only by precise timing belt synchronization. If the belt fails — from age (rubber breakdown), tensioner failure, or contamination by leaking front-engine oil seals — the camshafts stop while the crankshaft keeps spinning, and valves slam into pistons. Result: bent valves, often damaged guides, sometimes a cracked piston, and a repair bill that exceeds the car's value. Honda's published interval is 90,000 miles or 72 months, whichever comes first — and on 30+ year-old Legends 'whichever comes first' is almost always the calendar. Most original belts have been replaced by now, but second and third belts (60-90k after the first replacement) are commonly skipped because owners assume 'it's been done.'
records.solution: Replace the timing belt every 90,000 miles OR 72 months — and treat the 72-month limit as the binding one on cars over 15 years old, regardless of mileage. The job is a full front-of-engine teardown: remove crank pulley, front cover, all accessory belts. While you're in there, ALWAYS replace the water pump, timing belt tensioner, all front seals (crank, cam, balance shaft), and idler pulley as a kit — the labor to replace any one of them later is 90% of the timing belt labor. Use OEM Mitsuboshi/Bando belts from Acura or top-tier aftermarket (Aisin, Gates Powergrip). Expect $600-1,000 in parts and $500-900 in labor at an independent. Skip the dealer ($1,500-2,000+) unless they're running a special.

Squealing or rumbling from the front of the engine (tensioner bearing failing)
Oil leak from front of engine soaking the timing cover (failed crank or cam seal)

records.title: ALB/ABS modulator pump times out and pressure sensor fails on NA1 NSX (1991-1999)
records.description: The first-generation NSX uses an Anti-Lock Brake (ALB) hydraulic modulator with a high-pressure pump, accumulator, and pressure sensor. The pump is designed to charge the accumulator and then stop within 120 seconds. When internal O-rings dry and the pump can no longer build pressure — or when the pressure sensor itself fails — the pump runs continuously for the full 120 seconds before timing out, the ABS warning light comes on, and the system disables. Once the system disables, the car still stops on its base brakes but loses ABS function entirely. Acura's North American service policy mandates replacing the modulator, pump, and accumulator as whole assemblies (about $2,100 in parts alone, $2,600 total dealer cost) — but the failure is almost always either a $100 O-ring set or a pressure sensor, both serviceable internally.
records.solution: Three repair paths, from cheap to expensive. (1) DIY O-ring rebuild with the SOS or egmCarTech kit ($105-200), which replaces the brake-fluid-resistant O-rings inside the modulator; the kit includes a bleeder T-wrench and 28-piece O-ring set. (2) Professional rebuild by a specialist (AutoECU, ScienceofSpeed, etc.) for around $795 — they pull the unit, replace O-rings and the pump motor brushes if worn. (3) Dealer full-assembly replacement at $2,100-2,600. There is also a documented upgrade path to swap the 1991-1999 NA1 modulator for the 2000-2005 NA2 unit using the SOS conversion kit, which simplifies the system and improves long-term reliability. Before any repair, check that the failure isn't simply rodent damage to the pump motor wires under the car — a blown ALB fuse from chewed wires presents the same way and costs $10 to fix.
symptoms: ABS / ALB warning light comes on and stays on
Pump runs continuously for about 120 seconds before timing out
Loss of ABS function; base brakes still work but no anti-lock
Audible pump motor cycling when ignition is on
Blown ALB fuse on repeated key cycles

records.title: Climate control unit display pixel fade and dead buttons (1991-1999 NA1)
records.description: The NSX climate control unit (CCU) sits in the center console and uses an LCD display plus push-buttons to set temperature and fan. Over time the LCD pixels fade — typically starting at the top of the display and progressing down — until the temperature setting is unreadable. Separately or simultaneously, individual buttons stop responding because the conductive carbon pads on the rubber button backs wear off, and the circuit board's electrolytic capacitors dry out and leak. Acura's only remedy is full CCU replacement, which is typically out of stock or back-order from Honda parts and was originally priced over $1,000. Several NSX specialists rebuild the existing CCU for $150-300 by replacing the LCD, button pads, and capacitors — the unit then works like new and the original equipment is preserved.
records.solution: Mail-in CCU repair from an NSX specialist is the standard fix. ScienceofSpeed, AutoTechRescue, SpeedoFix, NSXe-repair, and ModuleRepairPro all offer rebuild service for around $150-300 with 1-3 day turnaround. Removal is a 20-30 minute job at home — pop the armrest, shift knob, ashtray, and center console trim, then four screws hold the CCU. Reinstallation requires no programming or coding. Avoid full Acura CCU replacement: even when available, the part is over $1,000 and the rebuilt original works identically. Common rebuild scope: LCD module, all rubber button pads, electrolytic capacitors C1/C2/C3 on the main board, and reflow on heat-stressed solder joints.

records.title: Snap-ring transmission failure on 1991-1992 NSX (serial range J4A4-1003542 to J4A4-1005978)
records.description: A manufacturing defect in early NSX 5-speed manual transmissions cut the countershaft snap-ring groove inside the case slightly too wide. Under load the snap ring twists repeatedly until it shatters, releasing metal fragments into the gear set. The failure is limited to a specific production run of transmissions numbered J4A4-1003542 through J4A4-1005978, installed in some — but not all — 1991 and 1992 model year NSXs. VIN does not predict membership in the range because transmissions were not installed in VIN-sequential order; the transmission serial number must be checked directly on the case.
records.solution: Two paths: (1) Acura dealer transmission replacement runs about $7,000-7,500 in parts and labor — this swaps the entire assembly. (2) An NSX specialist (ScienceofSpeed, NSX Modified, etc.) can rebuild the existing transmission and replace the upper case half for around $2,500-4,675 depending on shop and gear set choice, saving $3,000-4,500 vs dealer. Preventive repair before failure (replacing the upper case while gears are still intact) is about 10 hours labor + $700 parts. If the snap ring has already shattered, debris in the gear oil mandates a full teardown — do not just refill and drive. Honda's original goodwill program tapered off sharply in 1999, so post-2000 repairs are owner-paid.

Loud crunch or mechanical grinding from transmission when snap ring fragments break loose
Metal particles visible in transmission fluid on drain
Difficulty engaging or popping out of 1st or 2nd gear
Transmission may eventually lock up entirely

records.title: Targa roof gaskets harden, wind noise increases and water leaks under heavy rain
records.description: The NSX-T (T = Targa, optional from 1995) uses two rubber gaskets mounted on the Targa roof panel — one above each side window — plus seals around the panel perimeter that mate to the body when the roof is installed. The rubber dries and hardens with age and UV exposure, and wind noise becomes pronounced at highway speed. Under heavy rain, water can enter between the two gaskets and the side-window glass, particularly when the car is in motion (chassis flex pulls the seal away from the glass). The seals can be replaced but Honda's installation procedure is genuinely complex — the factory service manual section runs six pages and calls for 0.5mm butyl tape, 3.0mm EPT sealer, and Honda sealant #08712-0004. DIY replacement frequently fails because the bedding and alignment require care. Regular treatment with Honda Shin-Etsu silicone grease (P/N 08798-9013) significantly extends life of the existing seals.
records.solution: Two stages. PREVENTIVE: clean the gaskets monthly with isopropyl alcohol, then apply Honda Shin-Etsu silicone grease (P/N 08798-9013) — this is the same grease used on the door weatherstripping and prevents drying-out. A small tube ($15-25) lasts years. If gaskets are already cracked or compression-set, REPLACE: OEM Honda Targa seals run $300-500 for the set. Use the exact butyl tape (0.5mm) and EPT sealer (3.0mm) called out in the service manual, plus sealant #08712-0004. Most NSX owners use an NSX specialist (ScienceofSpeed, Driving Ambition, NSX Modified) for the install — $400-700 in labor — rather than DIY, because the alignment determines water-tightness and a mis-bedded seal leaks worse than the old one.
symptoms: Noticeable wind noise at the Targa-panel-to-glass interface above 50 mph
Whistling from the side-window upper corner
Water dripping inside the cabin during heavy rain (especially driving)
Damp carpet or headliner near the A-pillar
Visible cracks, gaps, or compression-set on the rubber Targa gaskets

records.title: Distributor shaft seal leaks oil into cap, causes misfires (P0300-P0304) on 3.5L C35A
records.description: Like every C-series V6 Honda used in the 1990s and 2000s (Legend, NSX, CL, TL, RL all share the family), the RL's 3.5L C35A V6 has a distributor mounted at the back of the head and driven directly off the camshaft. Inside the distributor housing, an oil seal isolates the cam-driven shaft from the cap/rotor/electrical assembly above. By 100,000 miles the seal hardens, oil pressure forces engine oil past the shaft, and the cap fills with oil. Result: misfires (typically P0300 random plus individual cylinder codes P0301-P0306 since this is a V6), rough idle, hesitation. RepairPal explicitly lists distributor O-rings as one of the most common Acura RL oil leak points. The figure-8 oil cooler seal and oil filter housing gasket are the other two common leaks on this engine — diagnose carefully before assuming distributor. The C35A engine remained in the first-gen RL through the entire 1996-2004 production run, so this issue affects all years.
records.solution: There is no replaceable seal inside the distributor — the seal is between the rotating shaft and the bearing inside the cast housing. The only fix is replacing the whole distributor assembly. OEM Honda runs $400-700; Cardone remanufactured runs $150-250. While the distributor is out, also replace the distributor cap, rotor, and ignition wires — they're cheap and you're already at the parts. Inspect the cap and rotor on the old unit for oil contamination to confirm distributor was the source. If you also see leaks elsewhere (figure-8 cooler seal, oil filter housing), address those at the same time — they share access path. Total job: 2-3 hours independent shop.

Engine misfires, especially under load or after warm-up

Rough idle that smooths out with throttle

records.title: Timing belt + hydraulic tensioner replacement at 90k mi / 72 months — interference engine
records.description: The first-gen RL's 3.5L C35A V6 is part of the Honda C-series V6 family, which is widely documented as interference design (valves and pistons share rotational space, separated only by timing belt synchronization). The published timing belt interval is 105,000 miles or 84 months per the maintenance schedule. The hydraulic timing belt tensioner on this generation has been reported by independent shops as a known failure point: the internal oil seal leaks, the tensioner loses pressure, the belt can jump a tooth or two, and valves can hit pistons. Multiple sources caution that aftermarket tensioners have a worse failure rate than OEM Honda or Aisin — pay for the OEM-equivalent kit. Note: belt replacement intervals are sometimes quoted as shorter (90,000 mi) by independent shops as a conservative buffer, but the manufacturer-published interval per Acura is 105k/84 months for this engine family.
records.solution: Replace the timing belt, tensioner, water pump, idler pulley, and required front seals as one service. Match the kit to the 1996–1999 C35A application and verify the tensioner manufacturer before installation; no current AISIN TKH-022 application was verified. Never perform a belt-only service on this interference engine.
symptoms: Squealing or rattling from front of engine (tensioner bearing or pulley)
Coolant leak from timing cover (water pump weep)
Oil pooling at base of timing cover (failed crank seal)
Engine cranks but doesn't start after belt jumps a tooth
Loud metallic clatter on cranking (valves striking pistons after belt failure)

records.title: Consumer Reports rated the 1996 SLX 'Not Acceptable' for rollover risk in low-speed turns
records.description: In August 1996 Consumer Reports published rollover test results showing the 1996 Acura SLX (a rebadged Isuzu Trooper) tipped onto two wheels during avoidance-maneuver testing at low speeds. Consumer Reports issued the rare 'Not Acceptable' rating and publicly demanded Isuzu and Acura halt sales and recall the vehicles. The story was front-page news and devastated SLX/Trooper resale value for the rest of the production run. Acura/Isuzu pushed back, and NHTSA reviewed the issue but declined to find a defect — no recall was ever issued. The SLX continued to sell through 1999. Despite the no-defect ruling, the rating affects buyers searching for 'is the SLX safe' or 'Acura SLX problems' even today. Used buyers should know the body-on-frame chassis IS taller and narrower than typical Acuras, and rollover characteristic differs from car-based SUVs. The fundamental physics are unchanged from a 1996 Trooper.
records.solution: There is no mechanical fix because there's no mechanical defect — the Consumer Reports finding was a stability characteristic, not a failed part. Buyers and owners should: (1) know the vehicle's center of gravity is high; avoid emergency lane-change maneuvers above 35 mph if possible. (2) Keep the suspension and tires in spec — worn shocks and underinflated tires make rollover more likely on any tall SUV. (3) Use the OEM-spec tire size; oversized off-road tires raise the center of gravity further. (4) Modern stability control didn't exist on the SLX — drive accordingly. Used-buyer tip: the SLX/Trooper market is depressed permanently because of this story, which makes well-maintained examples a relative bargain — but go in eyes-open about the handling envelope.
symptoms: Vehicle leans noticeably in normal-speed cornering
Tendency to skip/hop in tight low-speed turns with rear axle
Two-wheel tip during emergency avoidance maneuvers (the original CR finding)
Wandering or instability in crosswinds at highway speeds

communityRecommendations.content: If you're buying used, know that NHTSA reviewed and declined to find a defect — but the body-on-frame chassis is genuinely tall and narrow. Drive accordingly: no emergency lane changes above 35 mph, keep tires at spec, keep shocks fresh.
Don't fit oversized off-road tires. The SLX is already at the edge of stable proportions; lifting it or adding 33+ inch tires makes the original CR finding more accurate, not less.

Used-buyer angle: the rollover story permanently depressed SLX/Trooper market values. A well-maintained one is genuinely cheap for what it is — but go in knowing the handling envelope and avoid spirited driving.

records.title: Rear differential whine + transfer case (BW4422) failures inherited from Isuzu Trooper platform
records.description: The SLX is a rebadged Isuzu Trooper, and inherits the same drivetrain failures that plague the Trooper. The rear differential develops a high-pitched whine, primarily under load at highway speed, caused by ring-and-pinion wear from imperfect gear mesh. Once the whine starts it progressively worsens; if ignored, the gears can strip. Separately, the Borg-Warner transfer case used in 1998-1999 SLX/Trooper has documented seal-leak and bearing-wear failures. CRITICAL FLUID NOTE: do not assume any specific fluid spec without checking your service manual — early sources circulated incorrect fluid specifications for the Borg-Warner transfer cases used in these vehicles. Always verify the correct fluid by manufacturer documentation or a Borg-Warner technical lookup before topping off — using the wrong fluid is a known cause of accelerated failure.
records.solution: REAR DIFF: If whine is noticed early, change the gear oil to fresh 80W-90 GL-5 and run a friction modifier. This will not stop existing wear but can slow it. Once whine is pronounced, the only durable fix is a remanufactured rear axle assembly ($800-1,400) or a rebuild of the existing ring and pinion ($1,200-2,000 at a specialist). TRANSFER CASE: Verify the manufacturer-spec fluid is being used — DO NOT default to motor oil or ATF without confirming. Check fluid level every oil change. If the case is whining or has external leaks, source the correct Borg-Warner rebuild kit by part number from your vehicle's exact model year + transmission combination — multiple BW transfer case variants were used across SLX/Trooper years and the parts are NOT interchangeable.

Whine that changes pitch with throttle (worse on gas, quieter coasting)
Transfer case howl or grinding in 4WD only
Fluid leaking from transfer case seals
Vibration through the floor at highway speed

records.title: 1999 3.2TL 5-speed auto was the start of the famous Acura V6 transmission failures
records.description: 1999 was the launch year of the 2nd-gen TL with the 3.2L J32A V6 and a new 5-speed automatic. This transmission family turned into one of the worst Acura defects of the early 2000s — torque converter failure, 3rd-gear clutch pack burn-up, blocked oil passages from debris, and complete failure became common. American Honda extended the transmission and torque converter warranties in 2003 (per TSB 02-027). The 1996-1998 TL uses the older 4-speed automatic which is generally reliable; the failure pattern is specifically the 5AT introduced for 1999. If you are car-shopping a 1999 TL, the model year alone does not tell you which transmission you have — the early-1999 carryover may have the older 4AT while the mid-year 2nd-gen launch got the 5AT. Check the build date and trans serial to know.
records.solution: If you own a 1999 TL with the 5AT and it's slipping, flaring on shifts, or showing harsh 1-2 / 2-3 changes: STOP driving aggressively immediately. The damage compounds quickly. Get a transmission specialist (not a dealer) to drop the pan and check for clutch material in the fluid. If found, the only durable fix is a rebuilt transmission ($2,500-4,000) — not a fluid change, not a solenoid swap. The original Honda warranty extension to 7/100k expired in 2006, so out-of-pocket cost is now on the owner. Many owners install an aftermarket transmission cooler with the rebuild — the original spec is undersized for the load and contributed to the failure pattern. Avoid 'flush' services — pressurized flushes on a worn transmission accelerate failure by dislodging clutch debris.

Harsh 'thunk' downshifts when slowing
Slipping in 3rd gear under load
Transmission shudder at highway cruise
Burnt-smell or dark transmission fluid
Check engine light with P0700-series transmission codes
Complete loss of forward drive (catastrophic stage)

communityRecommendations.content: Do NOT 'flush' a worn 5AT. Pressurized flushes dislodge clutch debris from the case and accelerate the death of a struggling transmission. Drop and fill with manual fluid changes only.
Always add an aftermarket transmission cooler with any rebuild. The factory cooler is undersized for this transmission's load and was a contributing factor to the original failure pattern.
When shopping a 1999 TL used, check the build date and transmission serial number. Cars built before the mid-year 2nd-gen launch have the older 4-speed and are far more reliable.

records.title: Infotainment System Lag, Freezing, and Crashes
records.description: The dual-screen infotainment system in first-generation TLX models suffers from severe lag, random freezes, and full system crashes requiring a restart. The upper navigation screen and lower touchscreen frequently lose sync, with Bluetooth audio dropping mid-stream and the backup camera failing to display.
records.solution: Update infotainment firmware to the latest version via USB or dealer update. If freezing persists after the update, the head unit may need replacement with the revised hardware. Performing a factory reset can temporarily resolve lag but the issue typically returns.
symptoms: Touchscreen unresponsive or extremely laggy
System reboots while driving
Bluetooth audio cuts out
Backup camera black screen
Navigation screen freezes mid-route

citations.title: AcuraZine.com — TLX infotainment lag and crash reports across 2015-2020 model years

communityRecommendations.content: Hold the power/volume knob for 10 seconds to force a hard reboot. This clears the cache and resolves most temporary freezes without needing a dealer visit.

records.title: AC Compressor Clutch Failure
records.description: The TSX AC compressor clutch bearing fails prematurely, typically between 80,000-120,000 miles. The clutch bearing seizes and causes a loud screeching noise when the AC is engaged, eventually leading to belt damage and complete loss of air conditioning.
records.solution: Replace the AC compressor clutch assembly or the entire compressor unit. Replace the serpentine belt if scored or damaged from the seized bearing. Evacuate and recharge the AC system. Install a new receiver/drier to prevent moisture contamination.
symptoms: Screeching noise when AC is turned on
AC works intermittently
Burning rubber smell from belt area
AC clutch not engaging visibly
Belt chirping at idle with AC on

citations.title: AcuraZine.com — TSX AC compressor clutch failure diagnosis and Denso vs. aftermarket comparison

communityRecommendations.content: If the clutch bearing just started making noise, replace the full compressor rather than just the clutch. The internal seals are likely compromised too, and you will pay labor twice when the compressor body fails six months later.

records.title: Timing belt + water pump + tensioner/adjuster at 90k mi — G25A1 interference engine
records.description: The Vigor's 2.5L 20-valve SOHC inline-5 (G25A1) is an interference engine, so timing-belt failure can bend valves. Honda's interval is 90,000 miles or 6 years. The belt tensioner/adjuster and water pump age with the belt; coolant at the base of the timing cover can indicate a failing pump seal and makes a complete, correctly matched timing service urgent.
records.solution: Replace the timing belt, belt tensioner/adjuster, water pump, idler, front seals, and accessory belts as one service. No complete current AISIN kit was verified for the G25A1, so source the exact components separately and use an OEM Honda or independently verified OEM-quality tensioner/adjuster. Avoid unverified no-name timing components.
symptoms: Coolant pooling at base of timing cover (water pump weep)
Squealing or rumble from front of engine (tensioner bearing)
Engine cranks but won't start after parking it overnight
Loud metallic clatter on attempted start (valves struck pistons)
Visible cracks or shiny glazed surface on belt when inspected

communityRecommendations.content: Skip the $40 cheap-import kits. Aftermarket tensioners on the G25A1 routinely fail within 10k miles. Use OEM Honda or an independently verified OE-quality application — labor cost dwarfs the parts savings.

records.title: DC Fast Charging Speed Inconsistency
records.description: The ZDX frequently charges at speeds well below its advertised 190 kW maximum DC fast charging rate, with many owners reporting peak rates of only 80-120 kW even on 350 kW chargers. The battery thermal management system appears to limit charging speed aggressively, and charging curves vary significantly based on battery state of charge, ambient temperature, and recent driving patterns.
records.solution: Precondition the battery by using the "Precondition for DC Fast Charging" feature in the infotainment system before arriving at a charger. Charge between 10-80% SoC for optimal speeds — the charging rate drops significantly above 80%. Avoid DC fast charging immediately after extended highway driving at high speeds. Acura continues to push OTA calibration updates to improve charging curve behavior.
symptoms: DC fast charge peaks at 80-120 kW instead of 190 kW
Charging speed drops rapidly after initial peak
Long charge times compared to advertised specs
Battery preconditioning inconsistent
Charge rate varies dramatically between sessions

citations.title: AcuraZine.com — ZDX DC fast charging speed test results and optimization tips

communityRecommendations.content: Set a charging waypoint in navigation 30 minutes before arriving at a DC fast charger. This triggers battery preconditioning and can improve peak charging speed by 40-60 kW. Cold battery = slow charging, even in mild weather.

records.title: Software and OTA Update Bugs
records.description: The all-electric ZDX built on the GM Ultium platform experiences various software bugs including phantom range estimates, delayed response from the touchscreen, and OTA updates that occasionally fail mid-install requiring a dealer visit to complete. The Google built-in infotainment system also loses connectivity to the Acura app intermittently.
records.solution: Keep the vehicle connected to Wi-Fi overnight to allow OTA updates to download and install completely. Perform a full system reset through the Settings menu if the touchscreen becomes unresponsive. Contact Acura Connected Services if OTA updates fail — the dealer can force-push updates via their diagnostic tools. Disable and re-enable the Acura app integration to restore remote connectivity.
symptoms: OTA update fails to install completely
Touchscreen freezes or lags
Range estimate fluctuates by 20+ miles
Acura app loses connection to vehicle
Climate controls unresponsive through touchscreen

citations.title: AcuraZine.com — ZDX Ultium software bugs tracker and OTA update version history

communityRecommendations.content: Leave the ZDX plugged in AND connected to home Wi-Fi overnight for OTA updates. The updates are large (several GB) and the car needs to be in Park with sufficient battery to complete installation. Failed updates usually just need a stable connection.
